title: Ezekiel 22:23–31
context: In a third word, the LORD tells Ezekiel to declare that the land is uncleansed (22:24) and surveys its leaders: prophets like a roaring lion (22:25), priests who profane his holy things (22:26), princes like wolves (22:27), prophets who plaster with whitewash (22:28), and the people of the land, who oppress the poor and the foreigner (22:29). Zephaniah 3:3–4 has a similar list, and the whitewash image recalls Ezekiel 13:10–16; these are named without harmonizing. The LORD sought someone to “stand in the gap,” but found no one (22:30), so judgment falls (22:31).

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel reports, “The LORD’s word came to me, saying,” introducing the final oracle of the chapter. Arminian readers see a survey of every leading group in the land, showing how widely corruption had spread.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a third oracle beginning. Readers in this tradition note that this section moves through prophets, priests, princes, and people, leaving no group untouched by the indictment.

verses.text: “Son of man, tell her, ‘You are a land that is not cleansed nor rained on in the day of indignation.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, tell her, ‘You are a land that is not cleansed nor rained on in the day of indignation.’” Arminian readers see the land’s lack of rain as a sign of judgment and impurity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of an uncleansed land. Readers in this tradition note that rain often signals blessing in Scripture, so its absence here marks divine displeasure.

verses.text: There is a conspiracy of her prophets within it, like a roaring lion ravening the prey. They have devoured souls. They take treasure and precious things. They have made many widows within it.
verses.arminianNotes: “There is a conspiracy of her prophets within it, like a roaring lion ravening the prey.” Arminian readers see prophets who should guide the people instead devouring them for gain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see leaders acting like predators. Zephaniah 3:3–4 uses similar lion, wolf, prophet, and priest imagery, cited by reference, and readers in this tradition note the resemblance without harmonizing the two lists.

verses.text: Her priests have done violence to my law and have profaned my holy things. They have made no distinction between the holy and the common, neither have they caused men to discern between the unclean and the clean, and have hidden their eyes from my Sabbaths. So I am profaned among them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Her priests have done violence to my law and have profaned my holy things.” Arminian readers see priests failing in their duty to teach the difference between holy and common.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests neglecting their teaching role. Leviticus 10:10 gives priests the task of distinguishing holy and common, cited by reference, and readers in this tradition see the failure as grave.

verses.text: Her princes within it are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
verses.arminianNotes: “Her princes within it are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.” Arminian readers see rulers exploiting the people for profit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see princes acting as predators rather than protectors. Readers in this tradition note the link between violence and greed, showing how injustice serves personal gain.

verses.text: Her prophets have plastered for them with whitewash, seeing false visions, and divining lies to them, saying, ‘The Lord GOD says,’ when the LORD has not spoken.
verses.arminianNotes: “Her prophets have plastered for them with whitewash, seeing false visions.” Arminian readers see prophets covering the leaders’ sins with false assurances, echoing the whitewashed wall of 13:10–16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whitewash image from 13:10–16, cited by reference, applied here to prophets who claim “The Lord GOD says” when the LORD has not spoken. Readers in this tradition note the reuse without harmonizing the details.

verses.text: The people of the land have used oppression and exercised robbery. Yes, they have troubled the poor and needy, and have oppressed the foreigner wrongfully.
verses.arminianNotes: “The people of the land have used oppression and exercised robbery.” Arminian readers see corruption spreading beyond the leaders to the people, who oppress the poor, needy, and foreigner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see injustice reaching the whole community. Readers in this tradition note that the indictment holds ordinary people responsible too, not only their rulers and teachers.

verses.text: “I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I would not destroy it; but I found no one.
verses.arminianNotes: “I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I would not destroy it; but I found no one.” Arminian readers see no faithful leader among the prophets, priests, princes, and people of 22:25–29 willing to repair the breach. Many hear an echo of Moses (Psalm 106:23), and some apply the verse to Christ as the one who later stood in the gap.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse within this chapter: none of Judah’s leaders would repair the wall or intercede for the land. Many in this tradition also hear an echo of Moses standing “in the breach” (Psalm 106:23, which has its own existing box), and some apply the verse to Christ; these are held as applications, not the verse’s primary sense.

verses.text: Therefore I have poured out my indignation on them. I have consumed them with the fire of my wrath. I have brought their own way on their heads,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I have poured out my indignation on them … I have brought their own way on their heads,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers see judgment as the return of the people’s own choices upon them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s just judgment fitting the people’s deeds. Readers in this tradition note that the past-tense wording presents the judgment as certain, as though already accomplished.
